claim: Proteomic analysis identified 1298 proteins significantly upregulated in omental metastases compared to normal omentum, including ECM-related proteins dominated by collagens (COL1A1, COL3A1, and COL5A1), collagen-modifying hydroxylase (PLOD1 and PLOD2), and collagen-degrading matrix metalloproteinase (MMP2 and MMP9).
source: We identified total 1298 proteins significantly upregulated in omental metastases including several ECM-related proteins dominant by collagens (e.g. COL1A1, COL3A1, and COL5A1), collagen-modifying hydroxylase (PLOD1 and PLOD2), and collagen-degrading matrix metalloproteinase (MMP2 and MMP9) (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis data presented in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1a showing upregulated proteins in omental metastases.

claim: COL1A1, COL3A1, and COL5A1 are predictors of overall survival for EOC patients with hazard ratios of 1.16–1.20 (n = 2970).
source: Importantly, COL1A1, COL3A1, and COL5A1 have been correlated with disease progression (Gilkes et al., 2014) and are predictors of overall survival for EOC patients as shown in the pooled hazard ratio model obtained from CuratedOvarianData (HR 1.16–1.20, n = 2970) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by hazard ratio analysis from CuratedOvarianData dataset (n=2970) shown in Figure 1B, and cited literature (Gilkes et al., 2014).

claim: Collagen-encoding genes share a similar mRNA expression profile among normal omentum, ovary and fallopian tube based on Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA) of the GTEx dataset (n = 17,382).
source: Here, we identified that collagen-encoding genes share a similar mRNA expression profile among normal omentum, ovary and fallopian tube using the Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA) of the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) dataset (n = 17,382) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by GSVA analysis of GTEx dataset (n=17,382) shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Type I collagen (encoded by COL1A1 and COL1A2) shows the highest collagen gene expression in normal ovary and omentum as well as in the omental metastases.
source: In particular, type I collagen (encoded by COL1A1 and COL1A2) shows the highest collagen gene expression in normal ovary and omentum as well as in the omental metastases (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The origins of high COL1A1, COL1A2, and COL3A1 expression positively correlate with fibroblast-specific markers (FAP) and smooth muscle actin (ACTA2).
source: It is also noticed that the origins of high COL1A1, COL1A2, and COL3A1 expression positively correlate with fibroblast-specific markers (FAP) and smooth muscle actin (ACTA2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), whereas COL4A1, COL4A2, and COL18A1 seem to be predominantly expressed in ovarian cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Elevated ITGA2 expression positively correlates with the defined collagen gene set in TCGA (R = 0.32, p=1.2e-10) and GTEx (R = 0.34, p=1.9e-09) datasets.
source: Moreover, elevated ITGA2 expression positively correlates with the defined collagen gene set in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) (R = 0.32, p=1.2e-10) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–D) and GTEx (R = 0.34, p=1.9e-09) dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E) suggesting a potential interaction between ITGA2+ tumor cells and enriched collagens in the premetastatic niche.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA and GTEx datasets shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–E.

claim: 61.5% of patients-derived ascites-derived tumor cells (ATCs) are E-cadherin and ITGA2 positive.
source: Therefore, we examined whether ascites-derived tumor cells (ATCs) as well as matched primary (OV) and metastatic tissues (OM) express ITGA2, and identified that 61.5% of patients-derived ATCs are E-cadherin and ITGA2 positive. This finding suggests a potential advantage of elevated ITGA2+ tumor cells in promoting peritoneal dissemination to collagen-rich omentum (Figure 1F-G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence analysis of patient-derived ATCs shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: ITGA2 is the most prominent collagen-binding integrin expressed among the 47 reported EOC cell lines independent of their histological subtypes and TP53 status.
source: Here, ITGA2 is the most prominent collagen-binding integrin expressed among the 47 reported EOC cell lines independent of their histological subtypes and TP53 status (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic analysis of CCLE dataset shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ITGA2 mRNA expression of the EOC cell lines showed no significant correlation (R = −0.0012, p=0.99) to the suitability scores of serous histotype.
source: Although high-grade serous ovarian cancer is the most common and lethal histotype accounting for 60–70% of EOC death (Vaughan et al., 2011), ITGA2 mRNA expression of the EOC cell lines showed no significant correlation (R = −0.0012, p=0.99) to the suitability scores of serous histotype (Domcke et al., 2013; Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C and cited literature (Domcke et al., 2013; Vaughan et al., 2011).

claim: An overall high percentage of positive ITGA2 cytoplasmic (72.5%) and membranous staining (66%) of tumor cells was observed in 200 EOC patients without differences for histological grade, FIGO stage, and subtypes.
source: We observed an overall high percentage of positive ITGA2 cytoplasmic (72.5%) and membranous staining (66%) of tumor cells (total n = 200 EOC patients) without differences for histological grade, FIGO stage, and subtypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: Supported by tissue microarray data from 200 EOC patients shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: The mutational status of TP53 does not correlate with ITGA2 expression in patient-derived samples.
source: We also confirmed that the mutational status of TP53 does not correlate with ITGA2 expression in patient-derived samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 targeting of ITGA2 exon 29–30 resulted in a 743–747 bp homozygous deletion at the desired genomic locus.
source: The clonal selection of ΔITGA2 cells harboring a 743–747 bp homozygous deletion at the desired genomic locus was confirmed by genotyping PCR and Sanger DNA sequencing (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by genotyping PCR and Sanger DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Loss of total ITGA2 expression in ΔITGA2 cells was verified by western blot and its associated receptor integrin β1 (ITGB1) was unaltered in all the ΔITGA2 cells.
source: Loss of total ITGA2 expression in ΔITGA2 cells was verified by western blot (Figure 2E) and its associated receptor integrin β1 (ITGB1) was unaltered in all the ΔITGA2 cells.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Significantly reduced cell proliferation was observed in ∆ITGA2 cells only on collagen-coated plates, but not on classical plastic or fibronectin-coated plates.
source: Of note, significantly reduced cell proliferation was observed in ∆ITGA2 cells only on collagen-coated plates. In contrast, neither classical plastic nor fibronectin-coated plates showed such a difference (Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chemotaxis-induced cell motility was significantly reduced in ΔITGA2 cells.
source: Moreover, chemotaxis-induced cell motility was significantly reduced in ΔITGA2 cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by chemotaxis migration assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A significant increase of apoptotic (Annexin V+) and dead (DAPI+) cells was observed in OVCAR3, SKOV3, and IGROV1 ΔITGA2 cells under detachment-induced anoikis conditions.
source: Further investigation of cell detachment-induced anoikis, a critical step of tumor cells with enhanced mesenchymal features or undergoing malignant transformation, showed a significant increase of apoptotic (Annexin V+) and dead (DAPI+) cells in OVCAR3, SKOV3, and IGROV1 ΔITGA2 cells (*p<0.05; Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by anoikis assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Enhanced apoptosis in ΔITGA2 cells under non-adherent spheroid condition coincided with elevated levels of cleaved PARP.
source: The enhanced apoptosis in ΔITGA2 cells under non-adherent spheroid condition coincided with elevated levels of cleaved PARP, (Figure 3E) suggesting that ITGA2 promotes anoikis resistance in EOC cells.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing cleaved PARP levels in Figure 3E.

claim: The percentage of in vivo survival of ΔITGA2 cells was significantly decreased compared to WT in zebrafish xenograft model.
source: The percentage of in vivo survival of ΔITGA2 cells was significantly decreased compared to WT in all the tested EOC cells (Figure 3G), which is in line with the increased apoptosis of ΔITGA2 cells in the detachment-induced anoikis condition.
evidence: Supported by zebrafish xenograft survival data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Reduced tumor cell cluster formation was observed in ΔITGA2 of IGROV1 and SKOV3 compared to WT cells in zebrafish xenograft.
source: Interestingly, we observed reduced tumor cell cluster formation in ΔITGA2 of IGROV1 and SKOV3 compared to WT cells (Figure 3H-I).
evidence: Supported by zebrafish xenograft imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: The consistently strong cell adhesion efficiency to collagen type I, III, and IV in parental cell lines significantly diminished upon ITGA2 deletion.
source: Notably, the consistently strong cell adhesion efficiency to collagen type I, III, and IV in parental cell lines significantly diminished upon ITGA2 deletion. However, cell adhesion to laminin and fibronectin appeared in a cell line-dependent manner in ΔITGA2 cell lines which may be due to the redundancy of multiple integrin subunits. (Figure 4A-B).
evidence: Supported by ECM adhesion assay data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Constitutive overexpression of ITGA2 in ITGA2low cancer cell line (n = 4) significantly enhanced cell adhesion to collagen I and IV (p<0.001).
source: Vice versa, constitutive overexpression of ITGA2 in ITGA2low cancer cell line (n = 4) significantly enhanced cell adhesion to collagen I and IV (p<0.001; Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C) indicating a cell line-independent binding specificity of ITGA2 to collagen I, III, and IV.
evidence: Supported by cell adhesion assay data in ITGA2-overexpressing cells shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: ΔITGA2 cells failed to establish stable adhesion on collagen I as the surface area ratio remained <1 over time in time-lapse microscopy.
source: We observed that ΔITGA2 cells failed to establish stable adhesion on collagen I as the surface area ratio remained <1 over time (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cell-surface focal adhesion and expansion subcellular structure on bioprinted collagen was visualized in WT cells but not in ΔITGA2 cells by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis.
source: Cell-surface focal adhesion and expansion subcellular structure on bioprinted collagen was also visualized in WT cells but not in ΔITGA2 cells by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis. (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by SEM imaging shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The overall cell migration path on collagen was significantly elevated in ITGA2+ cells.
source: The overall cell migration path on collagen was also significantly elevated in ITGA2+ cells (Figure 4F), indicating that ITGA2 facilitates the dynamic interplay between cell-to-collagen adhesion and movement which may accelerate the passive dissemination in EOC metastasis.
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the percentage of ITGA2+ ATCs and the adhesion efficiency to type I collagen (R = 0.6858, p=0.0288) but not to fibronectin (R = −0.04, p=0.902).
source: Notably, there is no significant correlation between ITGA2 and ITGA5 expression in CCLE dataset (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The ECM ligand-receptor specificity was supported by a positive correlation between the percentage of ITGA2+ ATCs and the adhesion efficiency to type I collagen (R = 0.6858, p=0.0288) but not to fibronectin (R = −0.04, p=0.902) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of patient-derived ATCs shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TC-I-15 inhibitor specifically blocked ITGA2 interaction to collagen with marginal difference to fibronectin in EOC cell lines and patients-derived ATCs.
source: Furthermore, by treating EOC cell lines and patients-derived ATCs cells with the selective integrin α2β1 inhibitor TC-I-15. The inhibitor specifically blocked ITGA2 interaction to collagen with marginal difference to fibronectin (Figure 5C-E).
evidence: Supported by cell adhesion assay with TC-I-15 treatment shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Long-term treatment (10 days) with the TC-I-15 inhibitor showed no significant impact on cell proliferation and spheroid formation.
source: This inhibitory effect was not due to cytotoxicity of the drug itself since a long-term treatment (10 days) with the TC-I-15 inhibitor showed no significant impact on cell proliferation and spheroid formation (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by long-term treatment data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The ratio of cancer cell adhesion to mesothelial cells was significantly increased for 12 and 24 hr incubation (1.92- to 2.59-fold; WT/ ΔITGA2 cells).
source: The ratio of cancer cell adhesion to mesothelial cells was significantly increased for 12 and 24 hr incubation (1.92- to 2.59-fold; WT/ ΔITGA2 cells) (Figure 6A), supporting the role of ITGA2 in facilitating mesothelial cell adhesion.
evidence: Supported by cancer cell to mesothelial adhesion assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Among different types of ECM components, collagen markedly enhanced cancer spheroid invasion through the mesothelial monolayer.
source: Among the different types of ECM components, collagen markedly enhanced cancer spheroid invasion through the mesothelial monolayer (Figure 6B) which further supports the premetastatic role of collagen in cancer cell dissemination.
evidence: Supported by mesothelial clearance assay on different ECM substrates shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The mesothelial clearance ratio of ΔITGA2 spheroids was significantly reduced compared to WT cells in IGROV1, OAW42, and ES2 cells.
source: The mesothelial clearance ratio of ΔITGA2 spheroids was significantly reduced compared to WT cells in IGROV1, OAW42, and ES2 cells (Figure 6C-D) and vice versa markedly increased in ITGA2-OE spheroids in SKOV3ip cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by mesothelial clearance assay data shown in Figure 6C-D and 6E.

claim: A significant reduction of total tumor implants was observed in ΔITGA2 xenografts compared to WT xenografts after 8 weeks of intraperitoneal injection in mice.
source: Histological examination of peritoneal organs after 8 weeks revealed a significant reduction of total tumor implants in ΔITGA2 xenografts compared to WT xenografts (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The omentum harbors the highest number of metastatic foci compared to other organs in the peritoneal cavity in mouse xenograft model.
source: Moreover, a systematic microscopic examination revealed that the omentum harbors the highest number of metastatic foci compared to other organs in the peritoneal cavity reflecting the clinical observation that omentum is the most frequent site of metastasis (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: Supported by histological examination data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: 69 downregulated phosphoproteins were shared across all three ∆ITGA2 cell lines.
source: We identified 69 downregulated phosphoproteins shared across all three ∆ITGA2 cell lines (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomics analysis shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Gene ontological (GO) analysis classified that the enriched cell components in the biological process were related to cell organization, polarity, and GTPase activity.
source: Next, by applying the gene ontological (GO) analysis, we classified that the enriched cell components in the biological process were related to cell organization, polarity, and GTPase activity (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) and Reactome pathway analysis showed that MAPK1/3 activation and cell junction organization are significantly regulated through the ITGA2 axis.
source: Such observation was further supported by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) and Reactome pathway analysis showing that MAPK1/3 activation and cell junction organization are significantly regulated through the ITGA2 axis (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA and Reactome pathway analysis shown in Figure 7C–D.

claim: A total of 1061 phosphoproteins were significantly downregulated in IGROV1 ΔITGA2 cells.
source: Moreover, IGROV1 ΔITGA2 and WT cell was further analyzed because of the highest phosphoproteins detection in the mass spectrometry with a total of 18,471 phosphopeptides belonging to 3928 phosphoproteins. A total of 1061 phosphoproteins were significantly downregulated in ΔITGA2 (Figure 7E, and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomics analysis of IGROV1 cells shown in Figure 7E and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Unsupervised hierarchal clustering showed 20 downregulated proteins involved in the KEGG focal adhesion pathway (hsa04510) in ΔITGA2 cells.
source: Unsupervised hierarchal clustering of the significantly altered phosphoproteins showed 20 downregulated proteins involved in the KEGG focal adhesion pathway (hsa04510) (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: ITGA2 expression positively correlates with COL1A2, COL3A1, and COL5A1 involved in focal adhesion pathway in TCGA-ovarian cancer dataset.
source: In addition, transcriptomic analysis of the TCGA-ovarian cancer dataset revealed a positive correlation of ITGA2 expression to COL1A2, COL3A1, and COL5A1 involved in focal adhesion pathway (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic analysis of TCGA dataset shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cell junction adhesion proteins including E-cadherin and EpCAM were significantly upregulated in the ΔITGA2 EOC cells.
source: Consistent with proteomic profiling and western blot analysis, we confirmed that cell junction adhesion proteins including E-cadherin and EpCAM were significantly upregulated in the ΔITGA2 EOC cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Significantly decreased phosphorylation of MAPK3Y204 and MAPK1T185/Y187 were identified in ΔITGA2 condition.
source: In line with the phenotypic change of ΔITGA2 cells, significantly decreased phosphorylation of MAPK3Y204 and MAPK1T185/Y187, previously showing to inhibit its nuclear translocation and transactivation of cell proliferation signaling were identified in ΔITGA2 condition (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplements 1D and 2).
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplements 1D and 2.

claim: The phosphorylation of AKTS124 and AKTS129 are significantly reduced in the ΔITGA2 cells.
source: The phosphorylation of AKTS124 and AKTS129 are also significantly reduced in the ΔITGA2 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The phosphorylation of p-SrcY419 and FAK at sites Y397, Y577, S722, and S843 were significantly downregulated in ΔITGA2 condition.
source: The phosphorylation of the proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase p-SrcY419 as well as FAK at site Y397, Y577, S722, and S843 were also significantly downregulated in ΔITGA2 condition (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Defactinib treatment resulted in a significant reduction of p-FAKY397, p-FAKY576/577, and the downstream c-Raf, G1/S phase transition cyclin D1 expression.
source: Here, Defactinib treatment in EOC cells showed no impact on inhibiting the upstream p-Src419 but resulted in a significant reduction of p-FAKY397, p-FAKY576/577, and the downstream c-Raf, G1/S phase transition cyclin D1 expression (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of Defactinib treatment shown in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The inhibition of FAK phosphorylation by Defactinib led to a dramatic decrease in cell survival, anoikis resistance, and spheroid formation.
source: The inhibition of FAK phosphorylation by Defactinib led to a dramatic decrease in cell survival, anoikis resistance, and spheroid formation (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by functional assays with Defactinib treatment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A–D.

claim: Blockade of either FAK or MAPK signaling axis showed no direct impact of cell-collagen adhesion but significantly reduced mesothelial clearance activity of EOC cells.
source: Blockade of either FAK or MAPK signaling axis showed no direct impact of cell-collagen adhesion but significantly reduced mesothelial clearance activity of EOC cells, supporting the functional involvement of ITGA2, and FAK/MAPK axis in ovarian cancer metastasis model (Figure 7—figure supplement 3E–F).
evidence: Supported by cell adhesion and mesothelial clearance assays with inhibitors shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3E–F.

claim: EOC patients' samples revealed a remarkable upregulation of phosphorylated FAKY397,S843, and ERK1/2 T202/Y204 in ITGA2High omental metastases.
source: In line with phosphoproteomics and in vitro inhibition models, the EOC patients' samples also revealed a remarkable upregulation of phosphorylated FAKY397,S843, and ERK1/2 T202/Y204 in ITGA2High omental metastases (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of patient samples shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Peritoneal metastasis is the leading cause of mortality in epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) and results in a 17–39% 5 year survival rate.
source: Peritoneal metastasis is the leading cause of mortality in epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) and results in a 17–39% 5 year survival rate due to the majority of patients being diagnosed at advanced stage of disease (>75%, FIGO stage III/IV) (Halkia et al., 2012; Vaughan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Halkia et al., 2012; Vaughan et al., 2011).

claim: The majority of EOC patients are diagnosed at advanced stage of disease (>75%, FIGO stage III/IV).
source: Peritoneal metastasis is the leading cause of mortality in epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) and results in a 17–39% 5 year survival rate due to the majority of patients being diagnosed at advanced stage of disease (>75%, FIGO stage III/IV) (Halkia et al., 2012; Vaughan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Halkia et al., 2012; Vaughan et al., 2011).

claim: Collagens are major components of the ECM and account for ~90% of the total ECM.
source: Collagens are major components of the ECM and account for ~90% of the total ECM, not only providing structural integrity but also regulating diverse cellular functions (Gilkes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Gilkes et al., 2014).

claim: Dysregulation of collagens positively correlate with poor outcome in EOC patients.
source: Dysregulation of collagens positively correlate with poor outcome in EOC patients (Cheon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Cheon et al., 2014).

claim: Altered collagen organization influences tissue mechanics and compromises drug delivery.
source: Moreover, altered collagen organization also influences tissue mechanics and compromises drug delivery (Loeffler et al., 2006) thus contributes to the poor response to chemotherapy in EOC patients (Jazaeri et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Loeffler et al., 2006; Jazaeri et al., 2005).

claim: A subset of integrins (α1, α2, α10, and α11) exhibiting high collagen-binding affinity are responsible for transducing biochemical or mechanical cues to regulate cellular functions such as cell proliferation, adhesion, migration, and hemostasis.
source: A subset of integrins, namely α1, α2, α10, and α11 exhibiting high collagen-binding affinity, are responsible for transducing biochemical or mechanical cues to regulate a variety of cellular functions such as cell proliferation, adhesion, migration, and hemostasis (Adorno-Cruz and Liu, 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Adorno-Cruz and Liu, 2019).

claim: Integrin α5 (ITGA5) plays a critical role in mediating cancer cell interaction to fibronectin during peritoneal metastasis through a c-Met/FAK/Src-dependent signaling.
source: Recent studies highlight the critical role of integrin α5 (ITGA5) in mediating cancer cell interaction to fibronectin during peritoneal metastasis through an c-Met/FAK/Src-dependent signaling (Gao et al., 2019; Iwanicki et al., 2011; Kenny et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Gao et al., 2019; Iwanicki et al., 2011; Kenny et al., 2014).

claim: High-grade serous ovarian cancer is the most common and lethal histotype accounting for 60–70% of EOC death.
source: Although high-grade serous ovarian cancer is the most common and lethal histotype accounting for 60–70% of EOC death (Vaughan et al., 2011), ITGA2 mRNA expression of the EOC cell lines showed no significant correlation (R = −0.0012, p=0.99) to the suitability scores of serous histotype (Domcke et al., 2013; Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Vaughan et al., 2011).

claim: ITGA2 promotes cancer cell adhesion, anoikis resistance, and tumor spheroid-mediated mesothelial clearance in vitro as well as peritoneal metastasis in vivo.
source: Using multiple cell lines and patient-derived samples, we provide functional evidence that ITGA2 promotes cancer cell adhesion, anoikis resistance, and tumor spheroid-mediated mesothelial clearance in vitro as well as peritoneal metastasis in vivo.
evidence: Supported by multiple in vitro and in vivo experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ITGA2-dependent signaling is transduced by phosphorylation of focal adhesion kinase and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway.
source: (Phospho-)proteomics reveal that ITGA2-dependent signaling is transduced by phosphorylation of focal adhesion kinase and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Functional blockade targeting ITGA2-collagen mediated cell adhesion or inhibiting downstream focal adhesion kinase activity provides the basis of promising therapeutic potential for intervening with peritoneal metastasis.
source: Furthermore, functional blockade targeting ITGA2-collagen mediated cell adhesion or inhibiting downstream focal adhesion kinase activity provides the basis of the promising therapeutic potential for intervening with peritoneal metastasis.
evidence: Supported by functional inhibition experiments with TC-I-15 and Defactinib presented in the manuscript.
